draft.title: Reading graphs critically
card: First read the title, the axis labels and the scale. They tell you what the graph measures and in what units.
If a column graph's axis starts above zero, small differences look huge. The column heights no longer match the sizes of the values.
If the steps on an axis are not equal, such as 0, 10, 20, 50, a graph can look steady when it is not. Check that each step is the same size.
Example: in the graph above, Shop B's column looks twice as tall, but 100 is only 5 more than 95.

2.alt: A column graph of two shops' weekly sales. The axis starts at 90. Shop A is 95 and Shop B is 100. Shop B's column looks twice as tall as Shop A's.

draft.remember: Check the title, labels and scale before you trust the shape of a graph.

a.q: A column graph's axis starts at 90 instead of 0. What is the effect on how the graph looks?
a.why: Cutting off the bottom of the axis makes the columns shorter, so a small gap looks like a big one. The values themselves stay the same.
a.clue: Think about how tall the columns look compared with each other.

b.q: A line graph of a town's monthly rainfall has an axis marked 0, 10, 20, 50, 100 at equal spacing. Why is this misleading?
opts: The steps are unequal, so the line looks flatter than it is
The axis starts at zero, so changes look larger
The axis has too many numbers on it
The line graph should be a column graph
b.why: Equal spacing for unequal steps squashes the big jumps, so the rises look smaller than they are. Starting at zero is not a problem.
b.clue: Compare the size of each step on the axis.

b.best: The steps are unequal, so the line looks flatter than it is

check.summary: No problems found. The chart data matches the text: on an axis starting at 90, Shop A's column is 5 units tall and Shop B's is 10, so B's looks twice as tall.
